whyItExists.problem: Network requests, file reads, and timers take time. JavaScript can't freeze and wait — that would block the UI. Before Promises, async code used nested callbacks ('callback hell'), which was hard to read and error-prone.
whyItExists.solution: A Promise represents a value that will be available in the future — either fulfilled (success) or rejected (failure). .then() chains success handlers. .catch() handles errors. The chain is flat, readable, and composable.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any asynchronous operation: fetch API calls, reading files, setTimeout wrappers, database queries, geolocation.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Synchronous code doesn't need Promises. If you're writing new async code, prefer async/await (the next lesson) — it builds on Promises but reads like synchronous code.

explainModes.beginner: A Promise is a ticket for something that hasn't happened yet. When it succeeds, .then() runs. When it fails, .catch() runs. Think of ordering a pizza — the receipt is the promise, .then() is when the pizza arrives, .catch() is if they call to say they're out.
explainModes.simple: fetch('/api/user').then(res => res.json()).then(data => console.log(data)).catch(err => console.error(err)). Each .then() receives the return value of the previous one. .catch() handles any rejection in the chain.
explainModes.standard: Promises have three states: pending, fulfilled, rejected. .then(onFulfilled, onRejected) handles both. .catch(fn) is shorthand for .then(null, fn). .finally(fn) runs regardless of outcome. Promise.all([p1, p2]) waits for all; rejects if any rejects. Promise.race([p1, p2]) resolves/rejects with the first to settle. Promise.allSettled waits for all regardless of outcome.
explainModes.technical: Promises use microtask queue, which runs before the callback queue — after the current task but before setTimeout/setInterval callbacks. Chaining works because .then() always returns a new Promise. Throwing inside a .then() callback triggers the next .catch(). Unhandled rejections fire an 'unhandledrejection' event on window.
explainModes.deepDive: Promise implementations follow the Promises/A+ spec. The microtask queue (Promise, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) has priority over the macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval, requestAnimationFrame, I/O). This is why console.log after a resolved Promise fires before a setTimeout(fn, 0). Promise.withResolvers() (ES2024) exposes resolve/reject outside the constructor — useful for deferrable patterns.

questions.question: What does .catch() handle in a Promise chain?
options: Any rejection or thrown error in the chain above it
Only errors thrown in the Promise constructor
questions.explanation: .catch() catches any rejection or thrown error from any .then() earlier in the chain. It's equivalent to .then(null, errorHandler).

questions.question: What does Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]) do if p2 rejects?
options: Returns the results of p1 and p3
Waits for all then reports which failed
Returns undefined for p2 and continues
questions.explanation: Promise.all fails fast — if any promise rejects, the whole Promise.all rejects immediately with that error. Use Promise.allSettled if you need all results regardless of failure.

faq.a: An unhandled rejection logs a warning in the console. In Node.js, it can crash the process. Always add .catch() at the end of a chain. async/await makes this easier with try/catch.

faq.q: What is the difference between Promise.all and Promise.allSettled?
faq.a: Promise.all rejects immediately if any promise rejects. Promise.allSettled always waits for all promises and returns an array of {status: 'fulfilled'|'rejected', value|reason} — use it when you need all results even if some fail.

examples: Axios returns a Promise: axios.get('/api/users').then(r => r.data).catch(...)
Loading multiple resources in parallel: Promise.all([fetchUser(), fetchPosts()])
Geolocation: navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition wraps into a Promise for cleaner API
